name: Enron

summary.text: Enron Corporation was a Houston energy company whose collapse in late 2001 led to a federal Enron Task Force investigation. Its chief financial officer Andrew Fastow ran partnerships (LJM) and helped form a special purpose entity (Chewco) that kept debt and losses off Enron's books; the board waived its conflict-of-interest rules to allow this. Fastow pleaded guilty in January 2004 and cooperated; a Houston jury convicted former chief executives Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling on May 25, 2006. The SEC settled with J.P. Morgan Chase ($135 million) and Citigroup ($120 million) in July 2003 over prepay transactions that the SEC alleged disguised loans to Enron. Enron's auditor Arthur Andersen was convicted of obstruction of justice in 2002, a conviction the Supreme Court reversed in 2005.

facts.claim: On May 25, 2006 a federal jury in Houston convicted former Enron chief executives Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling: Lay on all six counts he faced, including conspiracy, wire fraud and securities fraud, and Skilling on 19 of 28 counts, with acquittal on nine insider trading counts; the verdict came after 56 days of trial before Judge Sim Lake.

facts.claim: Andrew Fastow, Enron's former chief financial officer, pleaded guilty on January 14, 2004 to two counts of conspiracy to commit securities and wire fraud, admitting that he conspired with senior management to cause Enron to enter improper transactions with the LJM entities he controlled; he agreed to cooperate and to a 10-year sentence.

facts.claim: The SEC alleged that between December 1997 and September 2001 J.P. Morgan Chase effectively loaned Enron approximately $2.6 billion through seven prepay transactions using Mahonia, an entity the SEC said was controlled by Chase and directed to participate ostensibly as an independent commodities-trading entity.
facts.quote: between December 1997 and September 2001, J.P. Morgan Chase effectively loaned Enron a total of approximately $2.6 billion in the form of seven such transactions

facts.claim: On July 28, 2003 the SEC settled with J.P. Morgan Chase, which agreed to pay $135 million ($65 million disgorgement, $5 million interest, $65 million penalties), and with Citigroup, which agreed to pay $120 million ($101.25 million allocable to Enron and $18.75 million to Dynegy) without admitting or denying wrongdoing; the SEC said $236 million would go to Enron fraud victims.
facts.quote: JPMorgan agreed to pay $135 million in disgorgement, penalties, and interest

facts.claim: Chewco was a special purpose entity created in 1997 by Fastow and others at Enron to buy CalPERS' stake in the JEDI partnership, keeping JEDI off Enron's balance sheet; Enron employee Michael Kopper owned and ran it, and Enron had to consolidate Chewco in 2001 because of the earlier improper accounting.
facts.quote: Fastow and others at Enron formed a special purpose entity called Chewco for this purpose

facts.claim: A House hearing record states that the Enron board waived its conflict of interest rules for Fastow to allow him partial ownership and managerial duties in Chewco and LJM while he remained on Enron's payroll; the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations examined the board's role in July 2002.
facts.quote: The Enron board waived Enron conflict of interest rules for Mr. Fastow to allow him partial ownership and managerial duties in Chewco and LJM while still on the payroll of Enron

facts.claim: The SEC alleged that the Raptor I entity, owned by Fastow's LJM2 partnership, was used to manipulate Enron's balance sheet and income statement and to generate profits for LJM2 and Fastow at Enron's expense; the Powers Report found Raptor owed Enron more than $700 million under hedging agreements and that Andersen billed Enron $5.7 million for advice on the LJM and Chewco transactions.
facts.quote: Andersen billed Enron $5.7 million for advice in connection with the LJM and Chewco transactions alone

facts.quote: It was part of President Bush's Corporate Fraud Task Force, created in July 2002.

facts.claim: The SEC said in 2004 that its review of trading before the September 11, 2001 attacks examined more than 9.5 million securities transactions and found no evidence that anyone with advance knowledge traded on it.

openQuestions: Site claim that JPMorgan Chase and Citigroup executed 'Mahonia/Yosemite prepay transactions, loans disguised as commodity sales': Mahonia is supported by the SEC's 2003 action against JPMorgan Chase; 'Yosemite' appears in private litigation records as credit-linked notes funding Citigroup prepays, not in the SEC release returned.

Site claim that Fastow 'hid $14B in debt inside Chewco/LJM SPEs': the $14 billion figure was not found; the SEC and congressional records describe Chewco, LJM1, LJM2 and the Raptors without that total.
Site claims of '$74 billion in shareholder equity erased', '20,000 employees stripped of pensions', and executives cashing out 'hundreds of millions' were not covered by the sources returned.
Enron's bankruptcy filing date (December 2001 per the site) was not confirmed by any source returned.

Site claim (9/11 entry) that the collapse of WTC 7 destroyed SEC evidence in the Enron inquiry: no source returned supports this; the Enron investigation proceeded to charges and convictions from 2002 to 2006.
